doc.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

title: Professors' attitude and the jazz heard in Rochester
summary: Faculty ignored jazz, though Jazz for Moderns and the Ridgecrest Inn brought in Miles, Brubeck, Dizzy and others.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: How did your professors feel about that? Or wasn’t it even an issue for them?

Well most of them didn’t really care. I went to class on time and did the homework. Some of them didn’t care for that kind of music so they didn’t like what I did in classes, and the school did not encourage a jazz profile. And the strange thing is at that time there was the Eastman Theater, there was a show called “Jazz for Moderns” that would travel throughout the country. And they played at the Eastman Theater, it was a wonderful auditorium, it seated maybe 2,000 people. And they had great bands going all through Rochester. And there was a place called the Ridgecrest Inn, where singles would work, and I remember Sonny Stitt as a sideman and I saw Horace play there with Art Farmer and Clifford Jordan and I saw Dizzy Gillespie’s band, I saw Carmen McRae’s band, I saw Oscar Peterson’s band. And for all the music in the town it seemed pretty strange that they would not acknowledge its existence. And at this “Jazz for Moderns” show that traveled down this same New York State Thruway, line, the show was Lambert, Hendricks and Ross, The Dave Brubeck Quartet, Maynard Ferguson Big Band with Wayne Shorter and Slide Hampton, and Miles’ band with ‘Trane and Philly and Paul, and Red Garland. So when you have that kind of music in town, with people who are THE © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
force in music, it’s hard to understand how a classical institution would continue to ignore its presence.
